[PAPER_0049, relevance_score=0.398] Hypotheses

Our main hypothesis for this experiment was that the magnitude of the adaptation response would be significantly different (either reduced or enhanced) in the synchronous speech group compared to the solo speech group. Thus, we predicted that while we would see a significant adaptation response at the group level in the solo speech group, adaptation may or may not be significant in the synchronous speech group.

[PAPER_0061, relevance_score=0.261] The additive model found no significant effect of group, β = -.457, t(28) = -0.131, p = .897. Therefore, our hypothesis that the synchronous speech group would show either significantly reduced or enhanced adaptation was not supported. Follow-up contrasts using estimated marginal means found that both groups showed a significant difference in adaptation between Block 3 and all other blocks, and between Block 7 and all other blocks (p < .002 in all cases, using the Tukey method for adjusting for multiple comparisons).

[PAPER_0075, relevance_score=0.265] The results do however suggest that synchronous speech resulted in increased between-participant variability in the magnitude and direction of the measured adaptation response. Exploratory analyses suggested the hypothesis that the effect of synchronous speech on adaptation may depend on the acoustic-phonetic properties of the accompanist voice; specifically, on whether the formant changes required for convergence aligned with those required for adaptation.

This matches the pattern of results for the synchronous speech group in Experiment 1.
items.paper_content_summary: The paper predicts significant solo-speech adaptation and a group difference in either direction, with no definite prediction for synchronous-speech adaptation [PAPER_0049]. It tests additive versus interactive models and reports block contrasts without stating the corresponding detailed predictions [PAPER_0060] [PAPER_0061]. Exploratory convergence analyses predict greater block effects in synchronous speech [FULLPAPER_0082] [FULLPAPER_0083].

[PREREG_0002, relevance_score=0.393] Data

Analytic Code

Materials

Papers

Supplements

Study Information

Hypotheses

Hypothesis 1: Participants in the solo speech group will show a significant adaptation response at the group level. We have no clear prediction for the extent or significance of adaptation in the synchronous speech group; adaptation may be significant or completely eliminated. Hypothesis 2: The magnitude of the adaptation response to a formant perturbation will be significantly different (reduced or enhanced) during the production of sentences in synchrony with another voice (synchronous speech) compared to production of sentences alone (solo speech).

[PREREG_0031, relevance_score=0.397] For (a), we predict that the solo speech group will show a significant effect of block, whereby blocks 3-6 will all differ from each other (with increasing adaptation), and blocks 6 and 7 will differ from each other (with compensation being greater in block 6 than block 7). We may or may not see the same pattern in the synchronous speech group. This part of the analysis will relate to hypothesis 1.

[PREREG_0032, relevance_score=0.440] This part of the analysis will relate to hypothesis 1. For (b), we predict that there will be a significant effect of group (either negative or positive), in which compensation values in both blocks 6 and 7 will either be significantly reduced or enhanced in the synchronous speech group relative to the solo speech group. This part of the analysis relates to hypothesis 2. Furthermore, we will use a chi-squared test on the frequency of adapters, followers and no-change participants in each group, to test whether there is an uneven distribution of participants across these categories in the two groups.

[PAPER_0023, relevance_score=0.392] Experiment 1

Method

Participants

Thirty participants (Mage = 22.53 years, SD = 4.15) took part in this experiment. We restricted our recruitment to females from the Southeast of England so as to match with the gender and accent of the accompanist voice used for the synchronous speech task (see Stimuli section). Demographic information on participants was collected via a self-report questionnaire.

[PAPER_0024, relevance_score=0.410] Demographic information on participants was collected via a self-report questionnaire. Participants were asked to tick one of four boxes (female, male, other, or prefer not to say) in response to the prompt "Are you:" All participants recruited for this study ticked the box for female. Participants were asked to report their native language via a free response box.

[PAPER_0026, relevance_score=0.345] An equal number of participants took part in the solo speech and synchronous speech conditions (15 in each). This sample size was chosen based on previous work in which significant sensorimotor adaptation in response to feedback perturbations is seen at the group level in groups of eight to 12 participants (Houde & Jordan, 1998; Lametti et al., 2018). We have chosen a sample size slightly higher than this per group, to increase sensitivity to potentially smaller effect sizes.

[PREREG_0039, relevance_score=0.367] Transformations

Inference criteria

The significance level for all statistical tests will be p = .05. This significance level will be corrected for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni method.

Data exclusion

Trial utterances in which a participant makes a significant speech error (e.g. only produces part of the sentence, re-starts the sentence, misses the sentence entirely) will be excluded from analysis. Whole datasets from a participant will be excluded if a participant makes significant speech errors on more than 10% of trials across the whole experiment.

[PREREG_0040, relevance_score=0.358] Additionally, whole datasets will be excluded from participants who show clear evidence of not having successfully completed the task of synchronisation in the synchronous speech group. This will be decided based on observation at the time of testing and clear evidence of an unusually high level of asynchrony in the dynamic time warping measure. Prior to data collection it is difficult to determine a sensible criterion for what constitutes an unacceptable level of asynchrony that would indicate misunderstanding or failure to comply with the task instructions.

[PREREG_0041, relevance_score=0.294] Assuming a normal distribution of asynchrony scores within our sample, we propose a cut-off score of more than 3 standard deviations above the group mean as an upper limit on asynchrony; however, we acknowledge that this may be subject to change depending on the distribution of asynchrony data we observe.

Missing data

Trials with missing formant frequency values will not be replaced. Our analyses will be sufficiently robust against missing datapoints, given that we will be excluding any participants with missing data on more than 10% of trials.

Exploratory analysis

[PAPER_0031, relevance_score=0.274] Stimuli

Sentence stimuli for the task were 50 sentences taken from the Harvard IEEE corpus of sentences (IEEE Subcommittee on Subjective Measurements, 1969). These sentences are designed to be phonetically balanced. Presentation of sentences was randomized within blocks. The accompanist voice audio stimuli used in the synchronized speech condition consisted of recordings of a female speaker of Standard Southern British English reading the same 50 sentences. These tokens were recorded using the internal microphone of a MacBook Air and the software program Audacity (Audacity Team, 2021).
items.paper_content_summary: Experiment 1 compared solo and synchronous speech between groups across seven blocks. The synchronous group spoke alone in Block 1 and with a prerecorded accompanist from Block 2. Both groups received the specified F1/F2 perturbation, ramped in Block 3, held through Block 6 and removed in Block 7. [FULLPAPER_0045] [FULLPAPER_0057] [FULLPAPER_0058]

[PREREG_0006, relevance_score=0.332] Study design

This study will involve a mixed design, with a between-subjects variable of group (solo speech versus synchronous speech) and a within-subjects variable of block (1-7). Participants will be assigned to either the solo speech or synchronous speech condition. Participants will read a series of sentences presented on a computer screen while wearing headphones and a headset microphone. Their speech will be fed back to them in real-time via headphones, either altered or unaltered.

[PREREG_0009, relevance_score=0.327] The structure of the experiment is illustrated in Figure 1. Feedback perturbation: To induce sensorimotor adaptation, a perturbation of the first two formants of the speech signal will be implemented and fed back to the participant in real-time. Formant frequencies in speech are crucial for the perceptual identification of vowels. This study will involve an upwards shift in F1 (by 49.5 mels) and a downwards shift in F2 (by 49.5 mels), resulting in a combined perturbation of 70 mels in F1/F2 space.

[PREREG_0015, relevance_score=0.535] Variables

Manipulated variables

This study involves two manipulated variables of group (synchronous speech versus solo speech) and block (1-7). The latter variable of block relates to whether speech feedback was altered or not (unaltered for blocks 1, 2 and 7; altered for blocks 3-6).

No files selected

Measured variables

Adaptation to the formant perturbation will be measured for each participant via two outcome variables: a production change measure and a vector of compensation measure.

[PAPER_0045, relevance_score=0.296] Quantification of Adaptation

To look at participant responses to the formant perturbation, firstly a production change measure was calculated for F1 and F2 separately by calculating the change in produced formant frequencies from Block 2 (baseline) to Block 6 (the final adaptation block) for each sentence; the mean was then taken across the 50 sentences to give an average production change value for each participant (for each formant).

[PAPER_0047, relevance_score=0.270] The angular difference between this inverse shift vector and a vector representing the participant's production change (relative to Block 2) was then calculated; the cosine of this difference was then multiplied by the magnitude of production change. This measure of adaptation thus quantifies the degree to which the observed change in produced formants (i.e., the production change measure above) precisely opposed the feedback perturbation. This measure was calculated for each individual trial and then averaged within each block after the introduction of the feedback perturbation (Blocks 3-7).

[PAPER_0071, relevance_score=0.269] This measure thus quantifies the extent to which the formant changes required for the participant to converge to the accompanist voice lay on the same vector as perfect compensation for the subsequent formant perturbation. Individual vectors of convergence are plotted in Figure 5D. A Pearson's correlation analysis found that this convergence-adaptation congruency measure was correlated with adaptation responses within individuals, r = .531, t(13) = 2.259, p = .042.

[PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.265] Acoustic Analysis

Speech was recorded at 16,000 Hz in MATLAB. Formant frequencies were analyzed using a custom-made script in Praat (Boersma & Weenink, 2021). First, the vocalized/periodic portions of the acoustic signal were isolated using Praat's autocorrelation method (Boersma, 1993; see Figure S1 in the online supplemental materials for an example).

[PAPER_0060, relevance_score=0.323] A random intercept model was run on adaptation values during Blocks 3 to 7, with fixed effects of block and group, and random intercepts of participant and sentence. Random slopes were not included since these resulted in failures of model convergence. Both an additive model (in which block and group had additive effects) and an interactive model (in which block and group had interactive effects) were tested; a likelihood ratio test found that the interactive model did not provide a better fit to the data, χ2(4) = 2.61, p = .625.

[PAPER_0061, relevance_score=0.293] The additive model found no significant effect of group, β = -.457, t(28) = -0.131, p = .897. Therefore, our hypothesis that the synchronous speech group would show either significantly reduced or enhanced adaptation was not supported. Follow-up contrasts using estimated marginal means found that both groups showed a significant difference in adaptation between Block 3 and all other blocks, and between Block 7 and all other blocks (p < .002 in all cases, using the Tukey method for adjusting for multiple comparisons).

[PAPER_0065, relevance_score=0.330] These changes are plotted in Figure 4. LMM analyses were run for each measure separately to test for interactions between group and block, with the hypothesis that the effect of block should be significantly greater for the synchronous speech group compared to the solo speech group (who performed the same solo reading task across the two blocks).

[PAPER_0067, relevance_score=0.318] No significant interaction was found for F1, β = 6.75, t(28.03) = 1.956, p = .061. To determine the significance of these changes, further LMM analyses were run on F0, F1, and F2 change (from Block 1 to Block 2), with the intercept suppressed (set to zero).

[PAPER_0045, relevance_score=0.271] Quantification of Adaptation

To look at participant responses to the formant perturbation, firstly a production change measure was calculated for F1 and F2 separately by calculating the change in produced formant frequencies from Block 2 (baseline) to Block 6 (the final adaptation block) for each sentence; the mean was then taken across the 50 sentences to give an average production change value for each participant (for each formant).

[PAPER_0047, relevance_score=0.284] The angular difference between this inverse shift vector and a vector representing the participant's production change (relative to Block 2) was then calculated; the cosine of this difference was then multiplied by the magnitude of production change. This measure of adaptation thus quantifies the degree to which the observed change in produced formants (i.e., the production change measure above) precisely opposed the feedback perturbation. This measure was calculated for each individual trial and then averaged within each block after the introduction of the feedback perturbation (Blocks 3-7).

[PAPER_0051, relevance_score=0.257] This measure was calculated for utterances from the second baseline block (Block 2), to establish task engagement and success before the feedback perturbation was introduced.

Firstly, spectrograms of the participant's and accompanist's productions for a given trial were calculated. Next, a similarity matrix was created using the cosine distances of the spectrogram magnitudes; dynamic programming was then used to find the lowest-cost "warp path" from one to the other (taking the accompanist's utterance as the "referent" to be warped onto).

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.207] This path was rotated to be expressed in the time domain and rescaled into seconds. The unsigned area under the curve was then taken as a measure of asynchrony between the two utterances, with higher values thus representing poorer synchrony (Ellis, 2003). These values were averaged across trials within Block 2 to give a mean asynchrony score for each participant. This was done for both solo speech and synchronous speech groups, in order to verify the expected difference in asynchrony scores according to which task was performed.

[PAPER_0070, relevance_score=0.276] To consider how convergence and adaptation may relate to one another, we looked at whether the required formant changes for convergence and adaptation were in the same or different directions for each participant in the synchronous speech group. To do this, a convergence-adaptation congruency measure was obtained using an identical calculation to that used for our measure of adaptation, but substituting the participant's formant changes from Block 2 to Block 6 with the difference between the participant's formants at Block 2 and the accompanist's formants.

[PAPER_0021, relevance_score=0.376] Transparency and Openness

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in this study. The design, hypothesis, and analysis for Experiment 1 were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/q86cj). Data and analysis scripts for both experiments are openly available on the Open Science Framework and can be accessed at: https://osf.io/gz87s/.

[PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.261] Acoustic Analysis

Speech was recorded at 16,000 Hz in MATLAB. Formant frequencies were analyzed using a custom-made script in Praat (Boersma & Weenink, 2021). First, the vocalized/periodic portions of the acoustic signal were isolated using Praat's autocorrelation method (Boersma, 1993; see Figure S1 in the online supplemental materials for an example).
